```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_knit$set(root.dir = normalizePath(".."))
knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo = FALSE,  message = FALSE,  warning = FALSE,  
                      dpi = 150, fig.path = "figures/04_")
```

**Objective**

Forecast next-week influenza incidence in Switzerland and assess whether 
Sentinella surveillance information improves predictive performance beyond 
mandatory reporting (Oblig), while comparing statistical and machine-learning 
forecasting approaches.

**Evaluation strategy**

- Expanding-window, rolling-origin evaluation across three test seasons 
(2023/24–2025/26).\
- Metrics: mean absolute error (MAE) and root mean squared error (RMSE), 
evaluated across all forecast weeks and during in-season weeks.\
- MAE skill score relative to the naive baseline:

  \[
  \text{MAE skill}=1-\frac{\text{MAE}_{\text{model}}}{\text{MAE}_{\text{naive}}}
  \]

  Positive values indicate lower MAE than the naive baseline, 
  zero indicates equal MAE, and negative values indicate higher MAE.

**Key comparison**

Model 1 (Negative Binomial GLM, Oblig-only) and Model 2 (Negative Binomial GLM, 
Oblig + Sentinella) are compared to assess whether Sentinella information 
improves one-week-ahead predictive performance. Model 3 uses Gradient Boosting, 
while Models 4a and 4b provide sensitivity analyses by adding COVID-season and 
post-2020 indicators, respectively.

# 1 Load data

```{r load_data, include=FALSE}
source("R/setup.R")

# Load packages
install_file <- "../install_packages.R"

# Load the national-level data
national <- load_national()

# Load the in-season classification from WP 4.2
in_season <- readr::read_csv("output/eda/in_season_weeks.csv",
                             show_col_types = FALSE)
```

The processed national dataset contains weekly influenza surveillance data from 
Oblig and Sentinella.\
The in-season classification identifies the weeks considered part of the 
influenza season.

```{r forecast_cache_setup, include=FALSE}
# Create the forecast cache directory.
forecast_cache_dir <- "../DataScienceInHealthcare/output/forecast_cache"

if (!dir.exists(forecast_cache_dir)) {
  dir.create(
    forecast_cache_dir,
    recursive = TRUE,
    showWarnings = TRUE
  )
}

# Models to rebuild; empty means reuse existing cache.
REBUILD_MODEL_CACHE <- character(0)


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Reusable cache for expensive model results
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------

get_or_build_cache <- function(cache_key, build_fn) {

  cache_file <- file.path(
    forecast_cache_dir,
    paste0(cache_key, ".rds")
  )

  # Reuse an existing result unless this cache key is marked for rebuilding.
  if (
    file.exists(cache_file) &&
    !(cache_key %in% REBUILD_MODEL_CACHE)
  ) {
    message("Loading cached result: ", cache_key)
    return(readRDS(cache_file))
  }

  # Otherwise, calculate the result and save it immediately.
  message("Building result: ", cache_key)

  result <- build_fn()

  saveRDS(result, cache_file)

  message("Saved cache: ", cache_file)

  result
}
```

# 2 Build the forecasting dataset

Purpose: Prepare the dataset for one-week-ahead forecasting by defining 
the forecast origin and next-week target, constructing lagged predictors, 
aligning target-week indicators, and identifying candidate predictors 
for model selection.

```{r model-specification-table}
model_spec_table <- data.frame(
  Component = c("Oblig AR terms", "Fourier terms","Sentinella lag",
                "Earlier Sentinella lags","Parameter selection"),
  `Candidate rules for the formal model` = c(
    "Consecutive lag combinations: 1; 1–2; 1–3; 1–4 weeks",
    "K = 1, 2, 3, corresponding to 1, 2, or 3 pairs of annual sine/cosine terms",
    "Forecast-origin observation preferred; previous-week observation as a conservative candidate",
    "Not included as default candidates in the main models",
    "Selected separately within each expanding training window"),
  Rationale = c(
    "Consistent with the original protocol's requirement for multiple autoregressive terms.",
    "Consistent with the original protocol's requirements for seasonality modelling and within-window selection.",
    "In WP 4.3, the same-week association was strongest, but evidence that Sentinella leads Oblig was insufficient.",
    "WP 4.3 showed no stable evidence of a 2–3-week lead.",
    "Avoids using the test seasons to select the model."), check.names = FALSE)

knitr::kable(model_spec_table, format = "pipe",
             caption = "Candidate rules and rationale for the forecasting models",
             align = c("l", "l", "l"))
```

```{r forecasting_dataset, include=FALSE}
# Step 1: Create one-week-ahead targets and candidate predictors
#
# Time-index convention:
#   origin = forecast-origin week t
#   prev1  = week t-1
#   prev2  = week t-2, etc.
#   target = week t+1
#
# Important:Predictors from the origin week may only be used if they are
# assumed to be available at the forecast origin.

forecast_data <- national |>
  dplyr::arrange(week_start) |>
  dplyr::mutate(
    # Forecast origin and target week
    origin_week = iso_week,
    origin_week_start = week_start,
    target_week = dplyr::lead(iso_week),
    target_week_start = dplyr::lead(week_start),

    # One-week-ahead target variables
    target_oblig_inc_100k = dplyr::lead(oblig_inc_100k),
    target_oblig_cases = dplyr::lead(oblig_cases),
    target_population = dplyr::lead(population),

    # Oblig incidence candidates:origin week and up to three preceding weeks
    oblig_origin = oblig_inc_100k,
    oblig_prev1 = dplyr::lag(oblig_inc_100k, 1),
    oblig_prev2 = dplyr::lag(oblig_inc_100k, 2),
    oblig_prev3 = dplyr::lag(oblig_inc_100k, 3),

    # Log-transformed Oblig incidence candidates
    oblig_log_origin = log1p(oblig_origin),
    oblig_log_prev1 = log1p(oblig_prev1),
    oblig_log_prev2 = log1p(oblig_prev2),
    oblig_log_prev3 = log1p(oblig_prev3),

    # Sentinella candidates:
    # same week as forecast origin and preceding weeks
    sent_origin = sentinella_ili_rate,
    sent_prev1 = dplyr::lag(sentinella_ili_rate, 1),
    sent_prev2 = dplyr::lag(sentinella_ili_rate, 2),
    sent_prev3 = dplyr::lag(sentinella_ili_rate, 3),

    # Log-transformed Sentinella candidates
    sent_log_origin = log1p(sent_origin),
    sent_log_prev1 = log1p(sent_prev1),
    sent_log_prev2 = log1p(sent_prev2),
    sent_log_prev3 = log1p(sent_prev3),

    # Fourier terms for the target week
    # K = 1, 2, or 3 can be considered during training-window selection
    target_season_week = dplyr::lead(season_week),
    sin1 = sin(2 * pi * target_season_week / 52),
    cos1 = cos(2 * pi * target_season_week / 52),
    sin2 = sin(4 * pi * target_season_week / 52),
    cos2 = cos(4 * pi * target_season_week / 52),
    sin3 = sin(6 * pi * target_season_week / 52),
    cos3 = cos(6 * pi * target_season_week / 52))

# Step 2: Attach the season classification of the target week

forecast_data <- forecast_data |>
  dplyr::left_join(
    in_season |>
      dplyr::select(iso_week, season, test_season, in_season) |>
      dplyr::rename(target_week = iso_week, target_season = season,
                    target_test_season = test_season, target_in_season = in_season),
                    by = "target_week")

# Step 3: Define candidate predictor sets for formal model selection

# Oblig auto-regressive candidates:
# choose a contiguous lag structure within each training window.
# The origin-week value corresponds to lag 1 relative to target week t+1.
oblig_ar_candidates <- list(
  AR1 = c("oblig_log_origin"),
  AR2 = c("oblig_log_origin", "oblig_log_prev1"),
  AR3 = c("oblig_log_origin", "oblig_log_prev1", "oblig_log_prev2"),
  AR4 = c("oblig_log_origin","oblig_log_prev1","oblig_log_prev2","oblig_log_prev3"))

# Fourier candidates: K = 1, 2, or 3
fourier_candidates <- list(
  K1 = c("sin1", "cos1"),
  K2 = c("sin1", "cos1", "sin2", "cos2"),
  K3 = c("sin1", "cos1", "sin2", "cos2", "sin3", "cos3")
)

# Sentinella candidates motivated by WP 4.3:
# origin week is the primary candidate only if available at origin;
# previous week is the conservative alternative.
sentinella_candidates <- list(
  origin = "sent_log_origin",
  previous_week = "sent_log_prev1"
)

# These objects define candidate sets only.
# Selection must be performed separately inside each training window.

# Step 4: Check missingness among the candidate predictors

all_candidate_predictors <- unique(c(
  unlist(oblig_ar_candidates, use.names = FALSE),
  unlist(fourier_candidates, use.names = FALSE),
  unlist(sentinella_candidates, use.names = FALSE)))

forecast_data |>
  dplyr::summarise(
    missing_target_incidence = sum(is.na(target_oblig_inc_100k)),
    missing_target_cases = sum(is.na(target_oblig_cases)),
    missing_target_population = sum(is.na(target_population)),
    missing_candidate_predictors = sum(
      !stats::complete.cases(
        dplyr::pick(dplyr::all_of(all_candidate_predictors))
      ))) |>
  print()

# Step 5: Check test-season weeks and their in-season classification

cat("Number of rows:", nrow(forecast_data), "\n")

forecast_data |>
  dplyr::filter(target_test_season %in% TRUE) |>
  dplyr::count(target_season, target_in_season) |>
  print()
```

The forecasting dataset contains `r nrow(forecast_data)` weekly observations. 
Missing target outcomes and candidate predictors were retained as missing rather 
than imputed. Observations were excluded from model fitting or evaluation when 
the variables required for the corresponding analysis were unavailable.

The number of in-season evaluation weeks varied across the three test seasons. 
The evaluation uses the target-week in-season classification and the common 
eligible forecast weeks.

**Target-week indicators and COVID-related data validation**

```{r indicators_validation, include=FALSE}
# =============================================================================
# Align COVID and post-2020 indicators with the target week
# =============================================================================

target_indicators <- national |>
  dplyr::select(iso_week, covid_season, post2020) |>
  dplyr::rename(target_week = iso_week, target_covid_season = covid_season,
                target_post2020 = post2020)

# Avoid joining the indicators twice if this block is re-run
forecast_data <- forecast_data |>
  dplyr::select(-dplyr::any_of(c("target_covid_season","target_post2020"))) |>
  dplyr::left_join(target_indicators,by = "target_week")

# Check indicator coverage and values
forecast_data |>
  dplyr::summarise(n_rows = dplyr::n(),missing_covid = sum(is.na(target_covid_season)),
                   missing_post2020 = sum(is.na(target_post2020))) |>
  print()

# Inspect the indicator types and values
str(forecast_data$target_covid_season)
str(forecast_data$target_post2020)

forecast_data |>
  dplyr::count(target_covid_season,target_post2020,.drop = FALSE) |>
  print(n = Inf)

# Identify the row with missing target-week indicators
forecast_data |>
  dplyr::filter(is.na(target_covid_season) | is.na(target_post2020)) |>
  dplyr::select(origin_week,target_week,origin_week_start,target_week_start,
                target_covid_season,target_post2020) |>
  print()

# Inspect the final rows of forecast_data
forecast_data |>
  dplyr::slice_tail(n = 5) |>
  dplyr::select(origin_week, target_week, origin_week_start, target_week_start,
                target_oblig_inc_100k, target_oblig_cases) |>
  print()

# Check rows without a valid one-week-ahead target
forecast_data |>
  dplyr::summarise(rows_without_target_week = sum(is.na(target_week)),
                   rows_without_target_date = sum(is.na(target_week_start)),
                   rows_without_target_incidence = sum(is.na(target_oblig_inc_100k)),
                   rows_without_target_cases = sum(is.na(target_oblig_cases))) |>
  print()
```

The COVID-related indicators were successfully mapped to the target weeks. Among 
the `r sum(!is.na(forecast_data$target_covid_season) & !is.na(forecast_data$target_post2020))` 
observations with valid target-week indicators, 
`r sum(forecast_data$target_covid_season %in% FALSE & forecast_data$target_post2020 %in% FALSE, na.rm = TRUE)` 
belong to neither the COVID seasons nor the post-2020 period, 
`r sum(forecast_data$target_covid_season %in% FALSE & forecast_data$target_post2020 %in% TRUE, na.rm = TRUE)` 
belong to the post-2020 period, and
`r sum(forecast_data$target_covid_season %in% TRUE, na.rm = TRUE)` 
belong to the COVID seasons.

The final row has no target week or target outcome because the dataset ends at 
the latest observed origin week. This is expected for one-week-ahead forecasting 
and does not indicate a data-joining error.

# 3 Define the forecasting methods and models

We compare two baseline forecasting methods with statistical and 
machine-learning models to assess the predictive value of Oblig incidence and 
the additional information provided by Sentinella. Model 1 is a Negative Binomial 
GLM using Oblig autoregressive predictors, while Model 2 additionally selects a 
Sentinella predictor. For both models, the autoregressive lag structure and 
Fourier terms are selected by AIC within each expanding training window. Model 3 
uses Gradient Boosting with the predictors selected by Model 2 in the same 
training window. Models 4a and 4b extend the combined Negative Binomial GLM with 
COVID-season and post-2020 indicators, respectively, as sensitivity analyses.

## 3.1 Rolling-origin expanding-window forecasts

**Purpose:** Rolling-origin expanding-window forecasts were generated for the 
predictive models across the three test seasons (2023/24, 2024/25, and 2025/26). 
At each forecast origin, the model was fitted using historical observations that 
met the training-data eligibility criteria and used to predict Oblig incidence 
one week ahead. The training window expanded as additional observations became 
eligible. To reduce the risk of using outcomes before they could reasonably 
have been observed, the training data were restricted to observations whose 
target week start date was at least seven days before the forecast origin.

Forecasts were evaluated on eligible test weeks with a common set of observed 
outcomes and predictors. Performance was assessed using MAE and RMSE and 
compared with the simple naive and seasonal naive baselines. Model specifications 
for the Negative Binomial GLMs were selected separately within each training 
window using AIC.

```{r rolling_origin_expanding_window_forecasts, cache=TRUE, include=FALSE}
# =============================================================================
# Rolling-origin expanding-window forecasts
# Models 1, 2, and 3
# =============================================================================

# Model 1: Oblig-only negative binomial GLM
# Model 2: Oblig + Sentinella negative binomial GLM
# Model 3: Gradient Boosting using Model 2's selected predictors

# -----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 1. Candidate predictors for NB GLM model selection
# -----------------------------------------------------------------------------

# Auto-regressive candidates: Oblig incidence observed at the forecast origin
ar_candidates <- list(
  AR1 = c("oblig_log_origin"),
  AR2 = c("oblig_log_origin", "oblig_log_prev1"),
  AR3 = c("oblig_log_origin", "oblig_log_prev1", "oblig_log_prev2"),
  AR4 = c("oblig_log_origin", "oblig_log_prev1", "oblig_log_prev2", "oblig_log_prev3"))

# Fourier candidates: K = 1, 2, or 3
fourier_candidates <- list(
  K1 = c("sin1", "cos1"),
  K2 = c("sin1", "cos1", "sin2", "cos2"),
  K3 = c("sin1", "cos1", "sin2", "cos2", "sin3", "cos3"))

# Sentinella candidates selected using the WP 4.3 analysis
sentinella_candidates <- c("sent_log_origin", "sent_log_prev1")

# -----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 2. Select the NB GLM specification within one training window
# -----------------------------------------------------------------------------

select_nb_model <- function(train_data, include_sent = FALSE) {

  # Use a common complete-case sample for all candidate specifications.
  # Model 1: Oblig predictors only.
  # Model 2: Oblig predictors plus one candidate Sentinella predictor.

  all_predictors <- unique(c(
    unlist(ar_candidates, use.names = FALSE),
    unlist(fourier_candidates, use.names = FALSE),
    if (include_sent) sentinella_candidates
  ))

  train_complete <- train_data |>
    dplyr::filter(
      !is.na(target_oblig_cases),
      is.finite(target_oblig_cases),
      target_oblig_cases >= 0,
      !is.na(target_population),
      is.finite(target_population),
      target_population > 0,
      dplyr::if_all(
        dplyr::all_of(all_predictors),
        ~ !is.na(.x) & is.finite(.x)
      )
    )

  if (nrow(train_complete) == 0) {
    stop("No complete training rows available for NB model selection.")
  }

  candidates <- list()
  fit_errors <- character()
  j <- 0L

  # Compare all AR lag and Fourier K combinations.
  # Model 2 additionally compares the predefined Sentinella candidates.

  for (ar_name in names(ar_candidates)) {
    for (fourier_name in names(fourier_candidates)) {

      sent_options <- if (include_sent) {
        sentinella_candidates
      } else {
        NA_character_
      }

      for (sent_var in sent_options) {

        predictors <- c(
          ar_candidates[[ar_name]],
          fourier_candidates[[fourier_name]],
          if (include_sent) sent_var
        )

        model_formula <- stats::as.formula(
          paste(
            "target_oblig_cases ~",
            paste(predictors, collapse = " + "),
            "+ offset(log(target_population))"
          )
        )

        fitted_model <- tryCatch(
          suppressWarnings(
            MASS::glm.nb(
              formula = model_formula,
              data = train_complete
            )
          ),
          error = function(e) {
            fit_errors <<- c(
              fit_errors,
              paste(
                ar_name,
                fourier_name,
                sent_var,
                conditionMessage(e),
                sep = " | "
              )
            )
            NULL
          }
        )

        if (!is.null(fitted_model)) {
          model_aic <- stats::AIC(fitted_model)

          if (is.finite(model_aic)) {
            j <- j + 1L
            candidates[[j]] <- list(
              model = fitted_model,
              formula = model_formula,
              predictors = predictors,
              AR = ar_name,
              Fourier = fourier_name,
              Sentinella = sent_var,
              AIC = model_aic
            )
          }
        }
      }
    }
  }

  if (length(candidates) == 0) {
    cat("Candidate NB GLM fitting errors:\n")
    print(utils::head(fit_errors, 10))
    stop("All candidate NB GLMs failed to fit.")
  }

  # Select the candidate with the lowest AIC.
  aic_values <- vapply(
    candidates,
    function(x) x$AIC,
    numeric(1)
  )

  best <- candidates[[which.min(aic_values)]]

  list(
    model = best$model,
    predictors = best$predictors,
    AR = best$AR,
    Fourier = best$Fourier,
    Sentinella = best$Sentinella,
    AIC = best$AIC,
    n_train = nrow(train_complete)
  )
}

# -----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 3. Define the common complete-case predictor set
# -----------------------------------------------------------------------------

# Models 1, 2, and 3 use the same eligible test weeks.
# This allows evaluation on common target weeks.

common_predictors <- unique(c(
  unlist(ar_candidates, use.names = FALSE),
  unlist(fourier_candidates, use.names = FALSE),
  sentinella_candidates
))


# Model 3 uses the predictors selected by Model 2
# separately within each training window.

# -----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 4. Expanding-window forecasting function
# -----------------------------------------------------------------------------

run_expanding_model <- function(
  data,
  model_type = c("NB_oblig", "NB_combined", "GBM"),
  model_name
) {

  model_type <- match.arg(model_type)

  # ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
  # 4.1 Select eligible test weeks
  # ---------------------------------------------------------------------------

  test_rows <- data |>
    dplyr::filter(
      target_season %in% TEST_SEASONS,

      !is.na(target_week_start),
      !is.na(week_start),

      !is.na(target_oblig_inc_100k),
      is.finite(target_oblig_inc_100k),

      !is.na(target_population),
      is.finite(target_population),
      target_population > 0,

      # Require all candidate predictors to be available.
      # This ensures a common evaluation sample across Models 1–3.
      dplyr::if_all(
        dplyr::all_of(common_predictors),
        ~ !is.na(.x) & is.finite(.x)
      )
    ) |>
    dplyr::arrange(target_week_start)

  if (nrow(test_rows) == 0) {
    stop("No eligible test weeks remain after filtering.")
  }

  # ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
  # 4.2 Generate one-week-ahead forecasts at each forecast origin
  # ---------------------------------------------------------------------------

  results <- vector("list", nrow(test_rows))

  for (i in seq_len(nrow(test_rows))) {

    new_data <- test_rows[i, ]

    # Forecast origin: start of the predictor week.
    origin_date <- as.Date(new_data$week_start[[1]])

  # Conservative training cutoff:
  # Only use observations whose target-week start date is at least
  # `cutoff_days` days before the forecast origin.
  # This corresponds to target weeks up to week t - (cutoff_days / 7).
  # The cutoff avoids assuming that the outcome for the forecast-origin
  # week (week t) is already available when the forecast is issued.
    
    train_data <- data |>
      dplyr::filter(
        !is.na(target_week_start),
        target_week_start <= origin_date - 7,

        !is.na(target_oblig_cases),
        is.finite(target_oblig_cases),
        target_oblig_cases >= 0,

        !is.na(target_oblig_inc_100k),
        is.finite(target_oblig_inc_100k),

        !is.na(target_population),
        is.finite(target_population),
        target_population > 0
      )


    # Initialise model-selection metadata.
    selected_AR <- NA_character_
    selected_Fourier <- NA_character_
    selected_Sentinella <- NA_character_
    selected_AIC <- NA_real_


    # -------------------------------------------------------------------------
    # 4.3 Models 1 and 2: Negative binomial GLM
    # -------------------------------------------------------------------------

    if (model_type %in% c("NB_oblig", "NB_combined")) {

      # Use the same complete-case training observations for both GLMs.
      common_train <- train_data |>
        dplyr::filter(
          dplyr::if_all(
            dplyr::all_of(common_predictors),
            ~ !is.na(.x) & is.finite(.x)
          )
        )

      if (nrow(common_train) == 0) {
        stop(
          "No common training observations at origin: ",
          as.character(origin_date)
        )
      }

      # Re-select the model specification inside this training window.
      if (model_type == "NB_oblig") {

        # Model 1: Oblig-only NB GLM.
        selected_model <- select_nb_model(
          train_data = common_train,
          include_sent = FALSE
        )

      } else {

        # Model 2: Combined Oblig + Sentinella NB GLM.
        selected_model <- select_nb_model(
          train_data = common_train,
          include_sent = TRUE
        )

      }

      fit <- selected_model$model

      # Save selected model structure for later auditing.
      selected_AR <- selected_model$AR
      selected_Fourier <- selected_model$Fourier
      selected_AIC <- selected_model$AIC

      if (model_type == "NB_combined") {
        selected_Sentinella <- selected_model$Sentinella
      }

      # Predict weekly case counts.
      predicted_cases <- stats::predict(
        fit,
        newdata = new_data,
        type = "response"
      )

      # Convert predicted counts to incidence per 100,000.
      prediction <- as.numeric(
        predicted_cases /
          new_data$target_population * 100000
      )

      n_train <- selected_model$n_train


    # -------------------------------------------------------------------------
    # 4.4 Model 3: Gradient Boosting using Model 2's selected predictors
    # -------------------------------------------------------------------------

    } else {

      # First select the Model 2 NB specification using this training window.
      # Reuse its selected predictors for Gradient Boosting.

      common_train <- train_data |>
        dplyr::filter(
          dplyr::if_all(
            dplyr::all_of(common_predictors),
            ~ !is.na(.x) & is.finite(.x)
          )
        )

      if (nrow(common_train) == 0) {
        stop(
          "No common training observations for Model 3 at origin: ",
          as.character(origin_date)
        )
      }

      selected_m2 <- select_nb_model(
        train_data = common_train,
        include_sent = TRUE
      )

      model3_predictors <- selected_m2$predictors

      # Store the same selected structure used by Model 2.
      selected_AR <- selected_m2$AR
      selected_Fourier <- selected_m2$Fourier
      selected_Sentinella <- selected_m2$Sentinella
      selected_AIC <- selected_m2$AIC

      # Gradient Boosting predicts incidence directly.
      model3_formula <- stats::reformulate(
        model3_predictors,
        response = "target_oblig_inc_100k"
      )

      gbm_train <- common_train |>
        dplyr::filter(
          !is.na(target_oblig_inc_100k),
          is.finite(target_oblig_inc_100k),

          dplyr::if_all(
            dplyr::all_of(model3_predictors),
            ~ !is.na(.x) & is.finite(.x)
          )
        )

      if (nrow(gbm_train) == 0) {
        stop(
          "No complete GBM training observations at origin: ",
          as.character(origin_date)
        )
      }

      set.seed(121)

      fit <- gbm::gbm(
        formula = model3_formula,
        data = gbm_train,
        distribution = "gaussian",
        n.trees = 500,
        interaction.depth = 2,
        shrinkage = 0.01,
        n.minobsinnode = 10,
        bag.fraction = 0.8,
        train.fraction = 1,
        verbose = FALSE
      )

      prediction <- as.numeric(
        stats::predict(
          fit,
          newdata = new_data,
          n.trees = 500,
          type = "response"
        )
      )

      n_train <- nrow(gbm_train)
    }


    # -------------------------------------------------------------------------
    # 4.5 Save forecast and model-selection metadata
    # -------------------------------------------------------------------------

    results[[i]] <- tibble::tibble(
      model = model_name,

      origin_week = as.character(
        new_data$iso_week[[1]]
      ),

      target_week = as.character(
        new_data$target_week[[1]]
      ),

      target_week_start = as.Date(
        new_data$target_week_start[[1]]
      ),

      target_season = as.character(
        new_data$target_season[[1]]
      ),

      target_in_season = new_data$target_in_season[[1]],

      actual = as.numeric(
        new_data$target_oblig_inc_100k[[1]]
      ),

      prediction = prediction,

      n_train = n_train,

      selected_AR = selected_AR,
      selected_Fourier = selected_Fourier,
      selected_Sentinella = selected_Sentinella,
      selected_AIC = selected_AIC
    )

  }


  # ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
  # 5. Return forecasts for all eligible test weeks
  # ---------------------------------------------------------------------------

  dplyr::bind_rows(results)
}
```

For model fitting, observations were restricted using the cutoff condition
`target_week_start <= origin_date - 7`, as implemented in the forecasting code. 
This restriction was intended to avoid using outcomes from target weeks that may
not yet have been available at the forecast origin. However, because reports are 
backfilled and historical data vintages are unavailable, actual data availability 
at each forecast origin cannot be verified.

## 3.2 Forecasting method 1 — Simple Naive Baseline

Purpose: Use the most recently observed Oblig incidence at the forecast origin 
as the prediction for the following week. This persistence baseline requires no
model fitting.

```{r forecasting method_1}
# Define the simple naive forecasting method
# Forecast next week's incidence using the latest observed incidence.

pred_method1 <- forecast_data |>
  dplyr::filter(target_test_season %in% TRUE) |>
  dplyr::transmute(
    method = "Simple naive",
    origin_week,
    target_week,
    target_week_start,
    target_season,
    target_in_season,
    actual = target_oblig_inc_100k,
    prediction = oblig_inc_100k
  )

# Keep forecasts with available observations and predictions for plotting
plot_method1 <- pred_method1 |>
  dplyr::filter(
    !is.na(actual),
    !is.na(prediction),
    !is.na(target_week_start)
  ) |>
  dplyr::arrange(target_week_start)

# Plot observed and predicted influenza incidence
ggplot2::ggplot(
  plot_method1,
  ggplot2::aes(x = target_week_start)
) +
  ggplot2::geom_line(
    ggplot2::aes(y = actual, color = "Observed"),
    linewidth = 0.7
  ) +
  ggplot2::geom_line(
    ggplot2::aes(y = prediction, color = "Simple naive forecast"),
    linewidth = 0.7,
    linetype = "dashed"
  ) +
  ggplot2::facet_wrap(
    ~target_season,
    scales = "free_x"
  ) +
  ggplot2::scale_x_date(                      
    date_breaks = "2 months",
    date_labels = "%b"
  ) +
  ggplot2::scale_color_manual(
    values = c(
      "Observed" = "#0B3C8C",
      "Simple naive forecast" = "#FDBF6F"
    )
  ) +
  ggplot2::labs(
    title = "Simple naive forecasting method",
    subtitle = "One-week-ahead forecasts during the test seasons",
    x = "Target week",
    y = "Oblig incidence per 100,000 population",
    color = NULL
  ) +
  ggplot2::theme_minimal() +
  ggplot2::theme(
    legend.position = "bottom"
  )
```

The naive forecast closely tracks the observed Oblig incidence in all three test 
seasons (2023/24, 2024/25, 2025/26). Because it simply carries forward the most 
recently observed value, it follows the overall seasonal trajectory but lags the 
observed series by about one week. This lag is most visible around the epidemic 
peak and on the rising and falling limbs, where the forecast underestimates 
during the rise and overestimates during the decline. Outside the influenza 
season, incidence is near zero and the forecast matches the observed values 
almost exactly.

## 3.3 Forecasting method 2 — Seasonal Naive Baseline

Purpose: Use the Oblig incidence observed 52 weeks before the target week as the 
forecast for the following week. This method provides a seasonal baseline for 
assessing whether more complex forecasting approaches improve predictive 
performance.

```{r forecasting method_2}
# Define the seasonal naive forecasting method
# Forecast next week's incidence using the incidence observed 52 weeks earlier.

seasonal_lookup <- national |>
  dplyr::transmute(
    seasonal_reference_week = week_start,
    seasonal_prediction = oblig_inc_100k
  )

pred_method2 <- forecast_data |>
  dplyr::filter(
    target_test_season %in% TRUE,
    !is.na(target_week_start)
  ) |>
  dplyr::mutate(
    seasonal_reference_week = target_week_start - 364
  ) |>
  dplyr::left_join(
    seasonal_lookup,
    by = "seasonal_reference_week"
  ) |>
  dplyr::transmute(
    method = "Seasonal naive",
    origin_week,
    target_week,
    target_week_start,
    target_season,
    target_in_season,
    actual = target_oblig_inc_100k,
    prediction = seasonal_prediction
  )

# Keep forecasts with available observations and predictions for plotting
plot_method2 <- pred_method2 |>
  dplyr::filter(
    !is.na(actual),
    !is.na(prediction),
    !is.na(target_week_start)
  ) |>
  dplyr::arrange(target_week_start)

# Plot observed and predicted influenza incidence
ggplot2::ggplot(
  plot_method2,
  ggplot2::aes(x = target_week_start)
) +
  ggplot2::geom_line(
    ggplot2::aes(y = actual, color = "Observed"),
    linewidth = 0.7
  ) +
  ggplot2::geom_line(
    ggplot2::aes(y = prediction, color = "Seasonal naive forecast"),
    linewidth = 0.7,
    linetype = "dashed"
  ) +
  ggplot2::facet_wrap(
    ~target_season,
    scales = "free_x"
  ) +
  ggplot2::scale_x_date(                      
    date_breaks = "2 months",
    date_labels = "%b"
  ) +
  ggplot2::scale_color_manual(
    values = c(
      "Observed" = "#0B3C8C",
      "Seasonal naive forecast" = "#FDBF6F"
    )
  ) +
  ggplot2::labs(
    title = "Seasonal naive forecasting method",
    subtitle = "One-week-ahead forecasts based on incidence\n52 weeks earlier",
    x = "Target week",
    y = "Oblig incidence per 100,000 population",
    color = NULL
) +
  ggplot2::theme_minimal() +
  ggplot2::theme(
    legend.position = "bottom",
    plot.subtitle = ggplot2::element_text(size = 10)
)
```

The seasonal naive forecast, based on incidence 52 weeks earlier, captures the 
general timing of the seasonal wave but agrees with the observed data less 
consistently. In 2023/24, it substantially overestimates the peak and places 
it earlier than observed. In 2024/25, it underestimates the peak magnitude. 
In 2025/26, the predicted peak occurs later than the observed one. These 
discrepancies reflect season-to-season variation in the timing and intensity of 
influenza activity, which a forecast based on the previous year cannot 
anticipate.

## 3.4 Model 1 — Negative Binomial GLM (Oblig-only)

Model 1 predicts Oblig incidence for the target week using reported Oblig cases. 
The response variable is `target_oblig_cases`, and a population offset is 
included to account for population size. Predicted case counts are converted to 
incidence per 100,000 population. At each forecast origin, AIC is used to select 
the autoregressive lag structure (AR1–AR4) and the number of Fourier terms (K1–K3) 
from the candidate specifications, using only the training data available at 
that origin.

```{r model_1_forecasts, include=FALSE}
# Model 1: Negative Binomial GLM (Oblig-only)
pred_model1 <- get_or_build_cache(
  "model1",
  function() {
    run_expanding_model(
      data = forecast_data,
      model_type = "NB_oblig",
      model_name = "Model 1: Negative Binomial GLM (Oblig-only)"
    )
  }
)

if (nrow(pred_model1) == 0) {
  stop("Model 1 returned no forecasts.")
}

# Check forecast completeness
model1_summary <- pred_model1 |>
  dplyr::summarise(
    n_forecasts = dplyr::n(),
    n_missing_actuals = sum(is.na(actual)),
    n_missing_predictions = sum(is.na(prediction)),
    n_non_finite_predictions = sum(
      !is.na(prediction) & !is.finite(prediction)
    )
  )

print(model1_summary)
```

### Interpretation of Model 1 Forecasts

Model 1 generated `r nrow(pred_model1)` one-week-ahead forecasts, with
`r sum(is.na(pred_model1$actual))` missing actual values, 
`r sum(is.na(pred_model1$prediction))` missing predictions, and
`r sum(!is.na(pred_model1$prediction) & !is.finite(pred_model1$prediction))` 
non-finite predictions.

At each forecast origin, AIC was used to select the auto-egressive lag structure 
and the number of Fourier terms using the eligible training data. The selected 
model structures were recorded for diagnostic and reproducibility purposes.

Note: The coefficient estimates, p-values, AIC, and theta reported below refer 
to the illustrative fit at the first test forecast origin. Forecasting 
performance is evaluated separately using the rolling-origin expanding-window 
procedure, with the model re-selected and refitted at each forecast origin.

```{r model_1_coefficients}
# Model 1: Negative Binomial GLM (Oblig-only)
# Extract coefficients, p-values, IRRs, and 95% confidence intervals.

model1_train <- forecast_data |>
  dplyr::filter(
    !is.na(target_week_start),
    target_week_start <= max(target_week_start, na.rm = TRUE) - 7
  )

model1_selected <- select_nb_model(
  train_data = model1_train,
  include_sent = FALSE
)

model1_fit <- model1_selected$model
model1_summary <- summary(model1_fit)$coefficients

# Calculate IRRs and confidence intervals on the unrounded estimates.
model1_coefficients <- as.data.frame(model1_summary) |>
  tibble::rownames_to_column("term") |>
  dplyr::rename(
    coefficient = Estimate,
    standard_error = `Std. Error`,
    test_statistic = `z value`,
    p_value = `Pr(>|z|)`
  ) |>
  dplyr::mutate(
    IRR = exp(coefficient),
    IRR_lower_95 = exp(coefficient - 1.96 * standard_error),
    IRR_upper_95 = exp(coefficient + 1.96 * standard_error)
  ) |>
  dplyr::mutate(
    dplyr::across(
      -term,
      ~ signif(.x, 4)
    )
  )

print(model1_coefficients, row.names = FALSE)
```

### Interpretation of Model 1 Coefficients

Model 1 uses a Negative Binomial GLM with a log link. Exponentiated coefficients 
are interpreted as incidence rate ratios (IRRs), conditional on the other 
predictors. The estimated coefficient for the specified Oblig predictor and its 
statistical significance should be interpreted in the context of the 
illustrative fit. The lagged incidence terms may be correlated, while the 
Fourier terms collectively represent seasonal patterns.

These coefficients describe conditional associations, not forecasting accuracy. 
Predictive performance is assessed separately using rolling-origin MAE and RMSE.

## 3.5 Model 2 — Negative Binomial GLM (Oblig + Sentinella)

Model 2 uses the same candidate autoregressive lag structures and Fourier terms 
as Model 1, while additionally selecting between `sent_log_origin` and
`sent_log_prev1`. Model selection is performed separately within each expanding 
training window using AIC, without using information from the future test period.

```{r model_2_forecasts, include=FALSE}
# Model 2: Negative Binomial GLM (Oblig + Sentinella)

# Generate expanding-window forecasts.
pred_model2 <- get_or_build_cache(
  "model2",
  function() {
    run_expanding_model(
      data = forecast_data,
      model_type = "NB_combined",
      model_name = "Model 2: Negative Binomial GLM (Oblig + Sentinella)"
    )
  }
)

# Check that forecasts were generated.
if (nrow(pred_model2) == 0) {
  stop("Model 2 returned no forecasts.")
}

# Inspect the first 10 forecasts.
pred_model2 |>
  dplyr::select(
    origin_week,
    target_week,
    target_season,
    actual,
    prediction,
    n_train,
    selected_AR,
    selected_Fourier,
    selected_Sentinella,
    selected_AIC
  ) |>
  print(n = 10, width = Inf)

# Calculate summary statistics using finite predictions only.
finite_predictions <- pred_model2$prediction[
  is.finite(pred_model2$prediction)
]

model2_summary <- pred_model2 |>
  dplyr::summarise(
    n_forecasts = dplyr::n(),
    n_missing_actuals = sum(is.na(actual)),
    n_missing_predictions = sum(is.na(prediction)),
    n_non_finite_predictions = sum(
      !is.na(prediction) & !is.finite(prediction)
    )
  ) |>
  dplyr::mutate(
    mean_prediction = if (length(finite_predictions) > 0) {
      mean(finite_predictions)
    } else {
      NA_real_
    },
    min_prediction = if (length(finite_predictions) > 0) {
      min(finite_predictions)
    } else {
      NA_real_
    },
    max_prediction = if (length(finite_predictions) > 0) {
      max(finite_predictions)
    } else {
      NA_real_
    }
  )

print(model2_summary)

# Inspect how often each model specification was selected.
model2_specification_counts <- pred_model2 |>
  dplyr::count(
    selected_AR,
    selected_Fourier,
    selected_Sentinella,
    name = "n_forecasts"
  ) |>
  dplyr::arrange(dplyr::desc(n_forecasts))

print(model2_specification_counts, n = Inf)
```

### Interpretation of Model 2 Forecasts

Model 2 generated 154 one-week-ahead forecasts, with no missing actual values, 
missing predictions, or non-finite predictions. At each forecast origin, the 
autoregressive lag structure, number of Fourier terms, and inclusion of lagged 
Sentinella information were selected using AIC within the eligible training data. 
The resulting predictions were used to evaluate out-of-sample performance using 
MAE and RMSE. The selected model specifications were recorded for diagnostic and 
reproducibility purposes.

**Note:** The coefficient estimates, p-values, AIC, and theta reported below 
refer to an illustrative model fit, rather than a summary of all rolling-origin 
fits. Forecasting performance is evaluated separately using the expanding-window 
rolling-origin procedure, with the model re-selected and refitted at each 
forecast origin.


```{r model_2_coefficients}
# Model 2: Negative Binomial GLM (Oblig + Sentinella)
# Extract coefficients, p-values, IRRs, and 95% Wald confidence intervals.
# Fit the illustrative model at the first eligible test forecast origin.

# Identify the first target week in the generated forecasts.
first_target_date <- pred_model2$target_week_start[[1]]

# Recover the corresponding forecast-origin row from forecast_data.
first_test_row <- forecast_data |>
  dplyr::filter(
    target_week_start == first_target_date
  ) |>
  dplyr::slice(1)

if (nrow(first_test_row) != 1) {
  stop("Could not identify the first test forecast row.")
}

# Use the same forecast-origin date and training cutoff as the forecasting function.
origin_date <- as.Date(first_test_row$week_start[[1]])

model2_train <- forecast_data |>
  dplyr::filter(
    !is.na(target_week_start),
    target_week_start <= origin_date - 7,

    !is.na(target_oblig_cases),
    is.finite(target_oblig_cases),
    target_oblig_cases >= 0,

    !is.na(target_oblig_inc_100k),
    is.finite(target_oblig_inc_100k),

    !is.na(target_population),
    is.finite(target_population),
    target_population > 0
  ) |>
  dplyr::filter(
    dplyr::if_all(
      dplyr::all_of(common_predictors),
      ~ !is.na(.x) & is.finite(.x)
    )
  )

if (nrow(model2_train) == 0) {
  stop("No eligible training observations for Model 2.")
}

# Select the combined NB GLM using the existing model-selection function.
model2_selected <- select_nb_model(
  train_data = model2_train,
  include_sent = TRUE
)

model2_fit <- model2_selected$model

# Extract coefficient estimates and standard errors.
model2_coef_raw <- as.data.frame(
  summary(model2_fit)$coefficients
) |>
  tibble::rownames_to_column("term") |>
  dplyr::rename(
    coefficient = Estimate,
    standard_error = `Std. Error`,
    test_statistic = `z value`,
    p_value = `Pr(>|z|)`
  )

# Calculate IRRs and 95% Wald confidence intervals.
model2_coefficients <- model2_coef_raw |>
  dplyr::mutate(
    IRR = exp(coefficient),
    IRR_lower_95 = exp(coefficient - 1.96 * standard_error),
    IRR_upper_95 = exp(coefficient + 1.96 * standard_error)
  ) |>
  dplyr::mutate(
    dplyr::across(
      -term,
      ~ signif(.x, 4)
    )
  )

print(model2_coefficients, row.names = FALSE)

# Report the selected model specification and diagnostics.
cat("Illustrative forecast origin:", as.character(origin_date), "\n")
cat("Selected AR structure:", model2_selected$AR, "\n")
cat("Selected Fourier terms:", model2_selected$Fourier, "\n")
cat("Selected Sentinella predictor:", model2_selected$Sentinella, "\n")
cat("Selected AIC:", model2_selected$AIC, "\n")
cat("Theta:", model2_fit$theta, "\n")
cat("Number of training observations:", model2_selected$n_train, "\n")
```

### Interpretation of Model 2 Coefficients

**Autoregressive predictors and seasonality.** The Oblig predictors describe 
conditional associations with the expected target-week case count. The Fourier 
terms represent recurring seasonal patterns.

**Sentinella predictor.** The estimated Sentinella coefficient and its 
confidence interval describe the conditional association between the selected 
Sentinella predictor and the expected Oblig case count, holding the other 
predictors constant.

**Predictive interpretation.** Whether Sentinella improves forecasting 
performance cannot be determined from its coefficient or p-value alone. This is 
assessed by comparing Model 2 with Model 1 on common rolling-origin test weeks 
using MAE and RMSE.

## 3.6 Model 3 — Gradient Boosting

At each forecast origin, the AIC-based predictor selection procedure used in 
Model 2 is applied first. The selected predictor set is then used to fit the 
Gradient Boosting model. Unlike Model 2, which models case counts using a 
Negative Binomial GLM with a population offset, Model 3 directly predicts
`target_oblig_inc_100k`. This allows the predictive performance of the two 
modelling approaches to be compared using the same rolling-origin evaluation 
framework and consistently selected predictors.

```{r model_3, include=FALSE}
# Model 3: Gradient Boosting
pred_model3 <- get_or_build_cache(
  "model3",
  function() {
    run_expanding_model(

      model_type = "GBM",
      model_name = "Model 3: Gradient Boosting"
    )
  }
)

  stop("Model 3 produced no forecasts. Check the test-season and training filters.")
}

# Keep only finite predictions for summary statistics
finite_predictions_model3 <- pred_model3$prediction[
  is.finite(pred_model3$prediction)
]

# Inspect forecasts and the predictor specification selected at each origin
pred_model3 |>
  dplyr::select(
    origin_week,
    target_week,
    target_season,
    actual,
    prediction,
    n_train,
    selected_AR,
    selected_Fourier,
    selected_Sentinella,
    selected_AIC
  ) |>
  print(n = 10, width = Inf)

# Summarise forecast coverage and prediction validity
model3_summary <- pred_model3 |>
  dplyr::summarise(
    n_forecasts = dplyr::n(),
    n_missing_actuals = sum(is.na(actual)),
    n_missing_predictions = sum(is.na(prediction)),
    n_non_finite_predictions = sum(
      !is.na(prediction) & !is.finite(prediction)
    ),
    mean_prediction = if (length(finite_predictions_model3) > 0) {
      mean(finite_predictions_model3)
    } else {
      NA_real_
    },
    min_prediction = if (length(finite_predictions_model3) > 0) {
      min(finite_predictions_model3)
    } else {
      NA_real_
    },
    max_prediction = if (length(finite_predictions_model3) > 0) {
      max(finite_predictions_model3)
    } else {
      NA_real_
    }
  )

print(model3_summary)
```

### Interpretation of Model 3 Forecasts

Model 3 generated `r nrow(pred_model3)` one-week-ahead forecasts, with
`r sum(is.na(pred_model3$actual))` missing actual values, 
`r sum(is.na(pred_model3$prediction))` missing predictions, and
`r sum(!is.na(pred_model3$prediction) & !is.finite(pred_model3$prediction))` 
non-finite predictions.

Among the finite predictions, predicted influenza incidence ranged from
`r if (any(is.finite(pred_model3$prediction))) sprintf("%.3f", min(pred_model3$prediction[is.finite(pred_model3$prediction)])) else "not available"` to `r if (any(is.finite(pred_model3$prediction))) sprintf("%.3f", max(pred_model3$prediction[is.finite(pred_model3$prediction)])) else "not available"` 
per 100,000 population, with a mean of 
`r if (any(is.finite(pred_model3$prediction))) sprintf("%.3f", mean(pred_model3$prediction[is.finite(pred_model3$prediction)])) else "not available"`.

At each forecast origin, the AIC-based predictor-selection procedure used in 
Model 2 selected the autoregressive lag structure, the number of Fourier terms, 
and the Sentinella predictor. The selected predictors were then used to fit the 
Gradient Boosting model, which directly predicts incidence per 100,000 
population rather than case counts.

Model 3 therefore combines the predictor-selection procedure used in Model 2 
with a different prediction algorithm. Its forecasting performance is evaluated 
using the same rolling-origin framework and compared with Model 1, Model 2, and 
the naive baselines using MAE and RMSE.

## 3.7 Model 4 — Sensitivity Analyses (COVID-Season and Post-2020 Indicators)

Model 4 comprises two sensitivity analyses based on Model 2, the Negative 
Binomial GLM using Oblig and Sentinella data. Model 4a adds a COVID-season 
indicator, while Model 4b adds a post-2020 indicator. Both models are evaluated 
using the same expanding-window forecasting framework to assess whether 
accounting for these periods changes predictive performance.

```{r model_4_sensitivity, include=FALSE}
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Model 4a and 4b: Sensitivity analyses
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------

run_nb_indicator_sensitivity <- function(data, indicator, model_name) {

  # Identify eligible one-week-ahead test forecasts.
  test_rows <- data |>
    dplyr::filter(
      target_season %in% TEST_SEASONS,
      !is.na(target_week_start),
      !is.na(week_start),
      !is.na(target_oblig_inc_100k),
      is.finite(target_oblig_inc_100k),
      !is.na(target_population),
      is.finite(target_population),
      target_population > 0,
      !is.na(.data[[indicator]]),
      dplyr::if_all(
        dplyr::all_of(common_predictors),
        ~ !is.na(.x) & is.finite(.x)
      )
    ) |>
    dplyr::arrange(target_week_start)

  if (nrow(test_rows) == 0) {
    stop("No eligible test weeks for ", model_name)
  }

  results <- vector("list", nrow(test_rows))

  for (i in seq_len(nrow(test_rows))) {

    new_data <- test_rows[i, ]
    origin_date <- as.Date(new_data$week_start[[1]])

    # Expanding training window; exclude information unavailable
    # at the forecast origin.
    train_data <- data |>
      dplyr::filter(
        !is.na(target_week_start),
        target_week_start <= origin_date - 7,
        !is.na(target_oblig_cases),
        is.finite(target_oblig_cases),
        target_oblig_cases >= 0,
        !is.na(target_oblig_inc_100k),
        is.finite(target_oblig_inc_100k),
        !is.na(target_population),
        is.finite(target_population),
        target_population > 0,
        !is.na(.data[[indicator]]),
        dplyr::if_all(
          dplyr::all_of(common_predictors),
          ~ !is.na(.x) & is.finite(.x)
        )
      )

    if (nrow(train_data) == 0) {
      stop(
        "No eligible training observations for ",
        model_name, " at origin: ",
        as.character(origin_date)
      )
    }

    # Select the base NB GLM specification using Model 2.
    selected_model <- select_nb_model(
      train_data = train_data,
      include_sent = TRUE
    )

    # Add the sensitivity indicator to the selected specification.
    sensitivity_predictors <- c(
      selected_model$predictors,
      indicator
    )

    sensitivity_formula <- stats::as.formula(
      paste(
        "target_oblig_cases ~",
        paste(sensitivity_predictors, collapse = " + "),
        "+ offset(log(target_population))"
      )
    )

    fit <- MASS::glm.nb(
      sensitivity_formula,
      data = train_data
    )

    predicted_cases <- stats::predict(
      fit,
      newdata = new_data,
      type = "response"
    )

    prediction <- as.numeric(
      predicted_cases /
        new_data$target_population * 100000
    )

    results[[i]] <- tibble::tibble(
      model = model_name,
      origin_week = new_data$week_start[[1]],
      target_week = new_data$target_week[[1]],
      target_week_start = new_data$target_week_start[[1]],
      target_season = new_data$target_season[[1]],
      target_in_season = new_data$target_in_season[[1]],
      actual = new_data$target_oblig_inc_100k[[1]],
      prediction = prediction,
      n_train = selected_model$n_train,
      selected_AR = selected_model$AR,
      selected_Fourier = selected_model$Fourier,
      selected_Sentinella = selected_model$Sentinella,
      selected_AIC = selected_model$AIC
    )
  }

  dplyr::bind_rows(results)
}
```

### Interpretation of Model 4 Sensitivity Analyses

**Model 4a: COVID-season indicator.**

Model 4a generated `r nrow(model4a_covid)` one-week-ahead forecasts across
`r dplyr::n_distinct(model4a_covid$target_season)` test seasons. The number of 
forecasts by season was
`r paste(paste0(names(table(model4a_covid$target_season)),": ", as.integer(table(model4a_covid$target_season))), collapse = "; ")`. 
Predicted incidence ranged from
`r round(min(model4a_covid$prediction, na.rm = TRUE), 3)` 
to `r round(max(model4a_covid$prediction, na.rm = TRUE), 3)` 
per 100,000 population, with a mean of
`r round(mean(model4a_covid$prediction, na.rm = TRUE), 3)`. 
This sensitivity model extends Model 2, the combined Oblig–Sentinella Negative 
Binomial GLM, by adding a COVID-season indicator. It assesses whether accounting 
for COVID seasons affects one-week-ahead forecasting performance.

**Model 4b: Post-2020 indicator.**

Model 4b generated `r nrow(model4b_post2020)` one-week-ahead forecasts across
`r dplyr::n_distinct(model4b_post2020$target_season)` test seasons. The number 
of forecasts by season was
`r paste(paste0(names(table(model4b_post2020$target_season)), ": ", as.integer(table(model4b_post2020$target_season))), collapse = "; ")`. 
Predicted incidence ranged from `r round(min(model4b_post2020$prediction, na.rm = TRUE), 3)` 
to `r round(max(model4b_post2020$prediction, na.rm = TRUE), 3)` 
per 100,000 population, with a mean of
`r round(mean(model4b_post2020$prediction, na.rm = TRUE), 3)`. 
This sensitivity model extends Model 2 by adding a post-2020 indicator, defined 
for the period from the 2022/23 season onward, to assess whether accounting for 
a potential level shift affects forecasting performance.

**Evaluation.** The two sensitivity models were evaluated across the test 
seasons. Their prediction distributions describe the range and central tendency 
of the forecasts but do not establish predictive superiority. Their performance 
should be compared with Model 2 using MAE and RMSE on common eligible target 
weeks.

## 3.8 Negative Binomial Model Diagnostics

The purpose of the convergence diagnostics was to assess whether the two primary 
Negative Binomial GLMs (Model 1: Oblig-only and Model 2: Oblig + Sentinella) 
could be fitted reliably across the expanding-window forecast origins. At each 
forecast origin, the selected predictor set was reconstructed and the 
corresponding model was refitted using eligible training data and the same 
conservative training cutoff as in the forecasting procedure.

For each fit, convergence status, fitting warnings, fitting errors, the 
estimated dispersion parameter (\(\theta\)), and Pearson residual dispersion 
were recorded. These diagnostics were used to identify potential numerical 
fitting problems and possible dispersion-related concerns. They do not, by 
themselves, establish overall model adequacy or predictive accuracy; forecasting 
performance was evaluated separately using MAE and RMSE.

The diagnostics focused on Models 1 and 2 because they are the two primary 
Negative Binomial GLMs. Model 3 uses Gradient Boosting and is therefore not 
subject to Negative Binomial GLM convergence diagnostics. Models 4a and 4b are 
sensitivity analyses and were outside the scope of this primary-model diagnostic 
check.

```{r model_diagnose, include=FALSE}
# =============================================================================
# Negative Binomial Model Diagnostics
# Check convergence of the two primary NB GLMs across forecast origins:
# Model 1: NB Oblig-only
# Model 2: NB Oblig + Sentinella
# =============================================================================

# Define the diagnostic function before using it.
diagnose_nb_convergence <- function(predictions, model_label) {

  diagnostic_results <- vector("list", nrow(predictions))

  for (i in seq_len(nrow(predictions))) {

    target_week_i <- predictions$target_week[i]
    target_week_start_i <- predictions$target_week_start[i]

    # Identify the forecast origin.
    new_data <- forecast_data |>
      dplyr::filter(
        target_week_start == target_week_start_i
      )

    if (nrow(new_data) != 1) {
      stop(
        "Expected exactly one row for target week: ",
        target_week_i,
        "; found ",
        nrow(new_data)
      )
    }

    origin_date <- as.Date(new_data$week_start[1])

    # Reconstruct the eligible training data using the same cutoff.
    train_data <- forecast_data |>
      dplyr::filter(
        !is.na(target_week_start),
        target_week_start <= origin_date - 7,
        !is.na(target_oblig_cases),
        is.finite(target_oblig_cases),
        target_oblig_cases >= 0,
        !is.na(target_oblig_inc_100k),
        is.finite(target_oblig_inc_100k),
        !is.na(target_population),
        is.finite(target_population),
        target_population > 0,
        dplyr::if_all(
          dplyr::all_of(common_predictors),
          ~ !is.na(.x) & is.finite(.x)
        )
      )

    # Reconstruct the predictor set selected at this forecast origin.
    selected_ar <- as.character(
      predictions$selected_AR[i]
    )

    selected_fourier <- as.character(
      predictions$selected_Fourier[i]
    )

    predictors <- c(
      ar_candidates[[selected_ar]],
      fourier_candidates[[selected_fourier]]
    )

    selected_sent <- as.character(
      predictions$selected_Sentinella[i]
    )

    if (
      length(selected_sent) > 0 &&
      !is.na(selected_sent) &&
      nzchar(selected_sent)
    ) {
      predictors <- c(predictors, selected_sent)
    }

    # Refit the selected Negative Binomial GLM.
    model_formula <- stats::as.formula(
      paste(
        "target_oblig_cases ~",
        paste(predictors, collapse = " + "),
        "+ offset(log(target_population))"
      )
    )

    fit_warnings <- character()
    fit_error <- NA_character_

    fit <- tryCatch(
      withCallingHandlers(
        MASS::glm.nb(
          formula = model_formula,
          data = train_data
        ),
        warning = function(w) {
          fit_warnings <<- c(
            fit_warnings,
            conditionMessage(w)
          )
          invokeRestart("muffleWarning")
        }
      ),
      error = function(e) {
        fit_error <<- conditionMessage(e)
        NULL
      }
    )

    # Record failed fits.
    if (is.null(fit)) {

      diagnostic_results[[i]] <- tibble::tibble(
        model = model_label,
        target_week = target_week_i,
        n_train = nrow(train_data),
        theta = NA_real_,
        converged = FALSE,
        pearson_dispersion = NA_real_,
        warnings = paste(
          unique(fit_warnings),
          collapse = " | "
        ),
        fit_error = fit_error
      )

    } else {

      residual_df <- stats::df.residual(fit)

      pearson_dispersion <- if (
        is.finite(residual_df) && residual_df > 0
      ) {
        sum(
          stats::residuals(fit, type = "pearson")^2
        ) / residual_df
      } else {
        NA_real_
      }

      diagnostic_results[[i]] <- tibble::tibble(
        model = model_label,
        target_week = target_week_i,
        n_train = nrow(train_data),
        theta = fit$theta,
        converged = isTRUE(fit$converged),
        pearson_dispersion = pearson_dispersion,
        warnings = paste(
          unique(fit_warnings),
          collapse = " | "
        ),
        fit_error = fit_error
      )
    }
  }

  dplyr::bind_rows(diagnostic_results)
}


# Run diagnostics using the existing cache.
# If the cache exists, the diagnostic models will not be refitted.
nb_diagnostics <- get_or_build_cache(
  "nb_diagnostics",
  function() {
    dplyr::bind_rows(
      diagnose_nb_convergence(
        predictions = pred_model1,
        model_label = "Model 1: NB Oblig-only"
      ),
      diagnose_nb_convergence(
        predictions = pred_model2,
        model_label = "Model 2: NB Oblig + Sentinella"
      )
    )
  }
)


# Summarise convergence, warnings, errors and dispersion.
nb_diagnostic_summary <- nb_diagnostics |>
  dplyr::group_by(model) |>
  dplyr::summarise(
    n_fits = dplyr::n(),
    n_not_converged = sum(!converged),
    n_fits_with_warnings = sum(warnings != ""),
    n_fit_errors = sum(!is.na(fit_error)),
    min_theta = if (all(is.na(theta))) {
      NA_real_
    } else {
      min(theta, na.rm = TRUE)
    },
    median_theta = if (all(is.na(theta))) {
      NA_real_
    } else {
      median(theta, na.rm = TRUE)
    },
    median_pearson_dispersion = if (
      all(is.na(pearson_dispersion))
    ) {
      NA_real_
    } else {
      median(pearson_dispersion, na.rm = TRUE)
    },
    .groups = "drop"
  )

print(nb_diagnostic_summary, n = Inf)


# Inspect any warnings or fitting errors.
nb_diagnostic_issues <- nb_diagnostics |>
  dplyr::filter(
    warnings != "" | !is.na(fit_error)
  ) |>
  dplyr::select(
    model,
    target_week,
    theta,
    converged,
    pearson_dispersion,
    warnings,
    fit_error
  )

print(nb_diagnostic_issues, n = Inf, width = Inf)
```

```{r model-diagnostics-output}
nb_diagnostic_summary |>
  dplyr::rename(
    Model = model,
    `Number of fits` = n_fits,
    `Non-converged` = n_not_converged,
    `Fits with warnings` = n_fits_with_warnings,
    `Fit errors` = n_fit_errors,
    `Minimum theta` = min_theta,
    `Median theta` = median_theta,
    `Median Pearson dispersion` = median_pearson_dispersion
  ) |>
  knitr::kable(
    digits = 3,
    caption = "Diagnostic summary for negative binomial models"
  )
```

### Interpretation of Diagnostic Results

**Model fitting diagnostics.** Model 1 (NB Oblig-only) was fitted across
`r nb_diagnostic_summary$n_fits[nb_diagnostic_summary$model == "Model 1: NB Oblig-only"]`
forecast origins, while Model 2 (NB Oblig + Sentinella) was fitted across
`r nb_diagnostic_summary$n_fits[nb_diagnostic_summary$model == "Model 2: NB Oblig + Sentinella"]`
forecast origins.

The median dispersion parameter (\(\theta\)) was
`r sprintf("%.2f", nb_diagnostic_summary$median_theta[nb_diagnostic_summary$model == "Model 1: NB Oblig-only"])`
for Model 1 and
`r sprintf("%.2f", nb_diagnostic_summary$median_theta[nb_diagnostic_summary$model == "Model 2: NB Oblig + Sentinella"])`
for Model 2. The corresponding median Pearson residual dispersion values were
`r sprintf("%.3f", nb_diagnostic_summary$median_pearson_dispersion[nb_diagnostic_summary$model == "Model 1: NB Oblig-only"])`
and
`r sprintf("%.3f", nb_diagnostic_summary$median_pearson_dispersion[nb_diagnostic_summary$model == "Model 2: NB Oblig + Sentinella"])`,
respectively.

These diagnostics summarise model fitting and residual dispersion across the 
evaluated forecast origins. They help identify potential numerical fitting 
issues and dispersion-related concerns but do not, by themselves, establish 
overall model adequacy or predictive accuracy. Predictive performance is 
assessed separately using MAE and RMSE.

# 4 Model Validation and Performance Comparison

Before evaluating predictive performance, forecast integrity was checked for 
both forecasting methods and all five models. The two forecasting methods were 
Method 1 (Naive) and Method 2 (Seasonal Naive). The five models comprised Model 
1 (Negative Binomial GLM using Oblig data only), Model 2 (Negative Binomial GLM 
using Oblig and Sentinella data), Model 3 (Gradient Boosting), and two 
sensitivity models: Model 4a (COVID-season indicator) and Model 4b 
(post-2020 indicator).

The integrity checks verified that each method and model produced forecasts, 
that target weeks were not missing, and that no duplicate predictions were 
generated for the same target week.

Predictive performance was evaluated using mean absolute error (MAE) and root 
mean squared error (RMSE), both overall and during influenza-season weeks. 
The evaluation was restricted to common target weeks with valid predictions from 
both forecasting methods and all five models. The distribution of common target 
weeks across test seasons is reported in the corresponding results table. 
Performance was also examined separately for each test season.

Method 1 (Naive) served as the reference for calculating the MAE skill score. 
A positive MAE skill score indicates a lower MAE than the Naive baseline, 
whereas a negative score indicates a higher MAE. Method 2 (Seasonal Naive) 
provided an additional benchmark based on observations from 52 weeks earlier. 
Both forecasting methods were evaluated alongside the five models.

The validation and performance evaluation assess forecast integrity and 
predictive accuracy, respectively. They do not, by themselves, establish that a 
model is universally superior or that its underlying assumptions are fully 
satisfied.

```{r models_validation, cache=TRUE, include=FALSE}
# =============================================================================
# Forecast validation: Check forecast integrity
# =============================================================================

prediction_list <- list(
  `Method 1: Naive` = pred_method1,
  `Method 2: Seasonal Naive` = pred_method2,
  `Model 1: NB Oblig-only` = pred_model1,
  `Model 2: NB Oblig + Sentinella` = pred_model2,
  `Model 3: Gradient Boosting` = pred_model3,
  `Model 4a: NB + COVID indicator` = model4a_covid,
  `Model 4b: NB + post-2020 indicator` = model4b_post2020
)

# Check that every method and model produced forecasts.
if (any(vapply(prediction_list, nrow, integer(1)) == 0)) {
  stop("At least one forecasting method or model produced no forecasts.")
}

# Check for missing target weeks.
if (any(vapply(
  prediction_list,
  function(x) any(is.na(x$target_week)),
  logical(1)
))) {
  stop("At least one forecasting method or model has missing target weeks.")
}

# Check for duplicate predictions per target week.
if (any(vapply(
  prediction_list,
  function(x) anyDuplicated(x$target_week) > 0,
  logical(1)
))) {
  stop("At least one forecasting method or model has duplicate predictions per target week.")
}

cat("Forecast integrity checks passed for both methods and all five models.\n")
```

```{r forecast_evaluation_metrics, cache=TRUE, include=FALSE}
# Check actual values before filtering invalid predictions.
actual_columns <- c(
  "actual",
  "actual_method2",
  "actual_model1",
  "actual_model2",
  "actual_model3",
  "actual_model4a",
  "actual_model4b"
)

actual_values <- as.matrix(validation_data[, actual_columns])

if (
  any(!is.finite(actual_values)) ||
  any(abs(actual_values - actual_values[, 1]) > 1e-8)
) {
  stop("Actual values are missing, non-finite, or differ across methods/models.")
}

# Keep common target weeks with finite predictions from every method/model.
validation_data <- validation_data |>
  dplyr::filter(
    dplyr::if_all(
      dplyr::starts_with("prediction_"),
      ~ is.finite(.x)
    )
  )

if (nrow(validation_data) == 0) {
  stop(
    "No common valid target weeks across both methods and all five models. ",
    "Check forecast coverage and missing predictions."
  )
}

cat(
  "Number of common valid target weeks across all methods and models:",
  nrow(validation_data),
  "\n"
)

# Remove duplicate actual-value columns after consistency checks.
validation_data <- validation_data |>
  dplyr::select(-dplyr::all_of(actual_columns[-1]))

# Report common evaluation weeks by test season.
common_weeks_by_season <- validation_data |>
  dplyr::count(target_season, name = "n_common_weeks")

print(common_weeks_by_season, n = Inf)

# =============================================================================
# Step 2: Reshape predictions into long format
# =============================================================================

validation_long <- validation_data |>
  tidyr::pivot_longer(
    cols = dplyr::starts_with("prediction_"),
    names_to = "model",
    values_to = "prediction"
  ) |>
  dplyr::mutate(
    model = dplyr::recode(
      model,
      prediction_method1 = "Method 1: Naive",
      prediction_method2 = "Method 2: Seasonal Naive",
      prediction_model1 = "Model 1: NB Oblig-only",
      prediction_model2 = "Model 2: NB Oblig + Sentinella",
      prediction_model3 = "Model 3: Gradient Boosting",
      prediction_model4a = "Model 4a: NB + COVID indicator",
      prediction_model4b = "Model 4b: NB + post-2020 indicator"
    ),
    abs_error = abs(actual - prediction),
    squared_error = (actual - prediction)^2
  )

# =============================================================================
# Step 3: Define overall and in-season evaluation groups
# =============================================================================

validation_groups <- dplyr::bind_rows(
  validation_long |>
    dplyr::mutate(evaluation = "All weeks"),

  validation_long |>
    dplyr::filter(target_in_season %in% TRUE) |>
    dplyr::mutate(evaluation = "In-season")
)

# =============================================================================
# Step 4: Calculate overall and in-season metrics
# =============================================================================

validation_metrics <- validation_groups |>
  dplyr::group_by(evaluation, model) |>
  dplyr::summarise(
    n = dplyr::n(),
    MAE = mean(abs_error),
    RMSE = sqrt(mean(squared_error)),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) |>
  dplyr::group_by(evaluation) |>
  dplyr::mutate(
    naive_MAE = MAE[model == "Method 1: Naive"][1],
    MAE_skill = 1 - MAE / naive_MAE
  ) |>
  dplyr::ungroup() |>
  dplyr::arrange(evaluation, MAE)

validation_metrics |>
  print(n = Inf, width = Inf)

# =============================================================================
# Step 5: Calculate metrics separately for each test season
# =============================================================================

validation_metrics_by_season <- validation_groups |>
  dplyr::group_by(evaluation, target_season, model) |>
  dplyr::summarise(
    n = dplyr::n(),
    MAE = mean(abs_error),
    RMSE = sqrt(mean(squared_error)),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) |>
  dplyr::group_by(evaluation, target_season) |>
  dplyr::mutate(
    naive_MAE = MAE[model == "Method 1: Naive"][1],
    MAE_skill = 1 - MAE / naive_MAE
  ) |>
  dplyr::ungroup() |>
  dplyr::arrange(evaluation, target_season, MAE)

validation_metrics_by_season |>
  print(n = Inf, width = Inf)
```

### Evaluation of Forecasting Performance

Across the common evaluation weeks, the five research models and two baseline 
methods were compared using MAE and RMSE, both overall and during in-season 
weeks. Lower MAE indicates smaller average absolute errors, while RMSE penalises 
larger errors more strongly. Model rankings may differ between these metrics and 
across test seasons. The results therefore describe performance on the evaluated 
weeks rather than guaranteeing future superiority.

# 5 Visualisation of Results

## Figure 1: MAE Comparison

```{r fig_1}
plot_mae <- validation_metrics |>
  dplyr::filter(evaluation == "All weeks") |>
  dplyr::mutate(
    model_type = dplyr::if_else(

      "Baseline methods",

  ) |>
  ggplot2::ggplot(
```

### Interpretation of Figure 1

Figure 1 compares the mean absolute error (MAE) of the five research models with 
the two baseline methods across the common evaluation weeks. Among the research 
models, the best-performing research model has the lowest MAE, followed by the 
second-best-performing research model. Performance is measured in cases per 
100,000 population.

The Naive baseline (Method 1) has an MAE that is reported in the corresponding 
results table, while the Seasonal Naive baseline (Method 2), which uses the 
observation from 52 weeks earlier, also has its MAE reported in that table. 
Comparing the research models with these baselines helps show whether the more 
complex forecasting approaches reduce average absolute prediction errors relative 
to simple reference methods.

The best-performing research model can be compared with Method 1 (Naive) using 
the MAE results reported in the corresponding results table. Figure 1 shows MAE 
only, so the ranking should also be considered alongside RMSE, which penalises 
larger forecast errors more strongly.

## Figure 2: MAE by Test Season

```{r fig_2 prepartion}
# Prepare Figure 2 interpretation data
research_models <- c(
  "Model 1: NB Oblig-only",
  "Model 2: NB Oblig + Sentinella",

)

fig2_data <- validation_metrics_by_season |>
  dplyr::filter(evaluation == "All weeks")

fig2_best_by_season <- fig2_data |>
  dplyr::filter(model %in% research_models) |>
  dplyr::group_by(target_season) |>
  dplyr::slice_min(MAE, n = 1, with_ties = FALSE) |>
  dplyr::ungroup()

fig2_naive <- fig2_data |>
  dplyr::filter(model == "Method 1: Naive") |>
  dplyr::select(target_season, naive_MAE = MAE)

fig2_seasonal_naive <- fig2_data |>
  dplyr::filter(model == "Method 2: Seasonal Naive") |>
  dplyr::select(
    target_season,
    seasonal_naive_MAE = MAE
  )

fig2_comparison <- fig2_best_by_season |>
  dplyr::select(
    target_season,
    best_model = model,
    best_MAE = MAE
  ) |>
  dplyr::left_join(fig2_naive, by = "target_season") |>
  dplyr::left_join(
    fig2_seasonal_naive,
    by = "target_season"
  ) |>

fig2_comparison
```

### Interpretation of Figure 2

Figure 2 shows that forecast accuracy varied across the three test seasons. 
Among the research models, **`r fig2_comparison$best_model[1]`** achieved the 
lowest MAE in
`r fig2_comparison$target_season[1]` (`r sprintf("%.2f", fig2_comparison$best_MAE[1])` 
per 100,000 population), **`r fig2_comparison$best_model[2]`** in 
`r fig2_comparison$target_season[2]` (`r sprintf("%.2f", fig2_comparison$best_MAE[2])`), 
and **`r fig2_comparison$best_model[3]`** in
`r fig2_comparison$target_season[3]` (`r sprintf("%.2f", fig2_comparison$best_MAE[3])`).

The Naive and Seasonal Naive methods provide reference benchmarks for each 
season. The results highlight seasonal variation in forecasting accuracy.

## Figure 3: Actual vs. Predicted Influenza Incidence

```{r fig_3}
# ---- 1. Define the model order ---------------------------------------------

plot_model_levels <- c(
  "Method 1: Naive",
  "Method 2: Seasonal Naive",
  "Model 1: NB Oblig-only",
  "Model 2: NB Oblig + Sentinella",
  "Model 3: Gradient Boosting",
  "Model 4a: NB + COVID indicator",
  "Model 4b: NB + post-2020 indicator"
)

# Check the actual model labels before plotting.
available_models <- unique(as.character(validation_long$model))

missing_models <- setdiff(plot_model_levels, available_models)

if (length(missing_models) > 0) {
  stop(
    "The following methods/models are missing from validation_long: ",
    paste(missing_models, collapse = ", "),
    "\nAvailable models: ",
    paste(available_models, collapse = ", ")
  )
}

# ---- 2. Create a target-week lookup -----------------------------------------

season_week_lookup <- validation_data |>
  dplyr::distinct(target_season, target_week) |>
  dplyr::mutate(
    iso_year = as.integer(substr(target_week, 1, 4)),
    iso_week = as.integer(sub(".*-W", "", target_week))
  ) |>
  dplyr::arrange(target_season, iso_year, iso_week) |>
  dplyr::group_by(target_season) |>
  dplyr::mutate(
    week_in_season = dplyr::row_number()
  ) |>
  dplyr::ungroup() |>
  dplyr::select(
    target_season,
    target_week,
    iso_week,
    week_in_season
  )

# ---- 3. Prepare prediction data ---------------------------------------------

Plot_Act.vs.Pre <- validation_long |>
  dplyr::filter(
    as.character(model) %in% plot_model_levels
  ) |>
  dplyr::left_join(
    season_week_lookup,
    by = c("target_season", "target_week")
  ) |>
  dplyr::mutate(
    model = factor(
      as.character(model),
      levels = plot_model_levels
    )
  ) |>
  dplyr::select(
    target_week,
    target_season,
    actual,
    prediction,
    model,
    iso_week,
    week_in_season
  )

# Keep one actual observation per target week and season.
Actual_Panels <- Plot_Act.vs.Pre |>
  dplyr::distinct(
    target_season,
    target_week,
    week_in_season,
    actual
  )

# ---- 4. Configure the peak-period x-axis ------------------------------------

brk <- seq(9, 29, by = 2)

lab <- c(
  "48", "50", "52", "2", "4", "6",
  "8", "10", "12", "14", "16"
)

# ---- 5. Print diagnostic information ----------------------------------------

message(
  "Number of methods/models: ",
  dplyr::n_distinct(Plot_Act.vs.Pre$model)
)

message("Prediction rows: ", nrow(Plot_Act.vs.Pre))

message(
  "Unique season-week combinations: ",
  nrow(season_week_lookup)
)

message(
  "Missing week indices: ",
  sum(is.na(Plot_Act.vs.Pre$week_in_season))
)

message(
  "Missing model labels: ",
  sum(is.na(Plot_Act.vs.Pre$model))
)

message(
  "Methods/models included: ",
  paste(
    levels(droplevels(Plot_Act.vs.Pre$model)),
    collapse = "; "
  )
)

# ---- 6. Create the plot -----------------------------------------------------

plot_figure3 <- ggplot2::ggplot() +
  ggplot2::geom_line(
    data = Actual_Panels,
    ggplot2::aes(
      x = week_in_season,
      y = actual,
      colour = "Actual"
    ),
    linewidth = 0.4,
    na.rm = TRUE
  ) +
  ggplot2::geom_line(
    data = Plot_Act.vs.Pre,
    ggplot2::aes(
      x = week_in_season,
      y = prediction,
      colour = "Prediction"
    ),
    linewidth = 0.4,
    na.rm = TRUE
  ) +
  ggplot2::geom_point(
    data = Plot_Act.vs.Pre,
    ggplot2::aes(
      x = week_in_season,
      y = prediction,
      colour = "Prediction"
    ),
    size = 0.4,
    na.rm = TRUE
  ) +
  ggplot2::facet_grid(
    rows = ggplot2::vars(model),
    cols = ggplot2::vars(target_season),

  ) +
  ggplot2::scale_x_continuous(
    breaks = brk,
    labels = lab,
    expand = ggplot2::expansion(mult = c(0.02, 0.02))
  ) +
  ggplot2::scale_y_continuous(
    breaks = c(0, 20, 40),
    expand = ggplot2::expansion(mult = c(0.05, 0.10))
  ) +
  ggplot2::scale_colour_manual(
    values = c(
      "Actual" = "#0B3C8C",
      "Prediction" = "#FDBF6F"
    )
  ) +
  ggplot2::coord_cartesian(
    xlim = c(9, 29)
  ) +
  ggplot2::labs(
    title = "Actual vs. Predicted Influenza Incidence",
    subtitle = paste(
      "Peak period (ISO weeks 48–16):",
      "two baseline methods and five research models"
    ),
    x = "ISO week of target week",
    y = "Incidence per 100,000",
    colour = NULL
  ) +
  ggplot2::theme_minimal(base_size = 8) +
  ggplot2::theme(
    plot.title = ggplot2::element_text(
      face = "bold",
      size = 10,
      hjust = 0.5
    ),
    plot.subtitle = ggplot2::element_text(
      size = 8,
      hjust = 0.5
    ),
    strip.text.x = ggplot2::element_text(
      face = "bold",

    ),
    strip.text.y.left = ggplot2::element_text(
      angle = 0,
      hjust = 1,
      size = 6,
      face = "bold",
      lineheight = 0.85
    ),
    strip.placement = "outside",
    strip.background = ggplot2::element_blank(),
    axis.title.x = ggplot2::element_text(size = 10),
    axis.title.y = ggplot2::element_text(size = 7),
    axis.text.x = ggplot2::element_text(size = 6),
    axis.text.y = ggplot2::element_text(size = 4.5),
    legend.position = "bottom",
    legend.text = ggplot2::element_text(size = 7),
    panel.grid.minor = ggplot2::element_blank(),
    panel.spacing = grid::unit(0.8, "lines"),
    panel.spacing.y = grid::unit(0.5, "lines"),
    plot.margin = ggplot2::margin(8, 10, 6, 8)
  )
```
