```{r fig_3}
print(plot_figure3)

```

### Interpretation of Figure 3

Figure 3 compares observed influenza incidence with one-week-ahead predictions 
from the two baseline methods and five research models during the peak period 
(ISO weeks 48–16) across the three test seasons.

The predictions from the Naive baseline (Method 1) reflect the most recently 
observed incidence level, while the Seasonal Naive baseline (Method 2) uses 
observations from 52 weeks earlier to reflect the corresponding seasonal pattern 
from the previous year. The degree of agreement between these baseline 
predictions and the observed incidence varies across test seasons.

Among the research models, the predicted trajectories differ in how closely they 
follow observed influenza activity and capture changes in incidence. Some models 
may overestimate or underestimate peak intensity in particular seasons. However, 
visual inspection alone cannot establish which model performs best 
quantitatively.

The quantitative evaluation complements this visual comparison. The MAE and RMSE 
results for the five research models and both baseline methods are reported in 
the corresponding evaluation results table. Because RMSE penalises larger errors 
more strongly than MAE, the model with the lowest MAE does not necessarily have 
the lowest RMSE.

Overall, Figure 3 provides a visual assessment of how closely the predicted 
incidence trajectories follow observed influenza activity during the peak period. 
Neither the visual patterns nor a single error metric alone establishes that one 
model is uniformly superior across all seasons and evaluation criteria.

# 6 Conclusion

This study evaluated one-week-ahead influenza incidence forecasting in 
Switzerland using an expanding-window rolling-origin approach across three test 
seasons (2023/24–2025/26). Two baseline methods were compared with five 
forecasting models, including two primary Negative Binomial GLMs, a Gradient 
Boosting model, and two sensitivity models incorporating COVID-season and 
post-2020 indicators. Predictive performance was assessed using MAE and RMSE 
across common evaluation weeks and during influenza-season weeks.

**Model 3 (Gradient Boosting) was the best-performing model in terms of overall MAE.** 
It achieved an MAE of 1.14 incidence per 100,000 population, outperforming the Naive 
baseline (1.31) and the Seasonal Naive baseline (3.17). It also achieved the 
lowest MAE among the research models in each of the three test seasons, with 
values of 1.04, 1.28, and 1.09 for 2023/24, 2024/25, and 2025/26, respectively. 
These results indicate that Gradient Boosting provided the most accurate 
forecasts in terms of average absolute error among the evaluated approaches.

The comparison between the two primary Negative Binomial GLMs showed that Model 
2, which incorporated Oblig and Sentinella information, achieved a lower overall 
MAE (5.61) than Model 1, which used Oblig data only (9.28). However, Model 2 
did not outperform the Naive baseline. Thus, although adding Sentinella 
information was associated with improved MAE relative to the Oblig-only GLM in 
this comparison, the results do not demonstrate that it consistently adds 
sufficient predictive value to outperform a simple persistence forecast. The 
sensitivity analyses also did not improve on the combined model: Model 4a, with 
a COVID-season indicator, achieved an MAE of 6.15, while Model 4b, with a 
post-2020 indicator, achieved an MAE of 9.59.

The visual comparison of observed and predicted incidence provided additional 
insight into model behaviour during influenza peaks. The Naive baseline followed 
recent incidence levels but could lag behind rapid changes, while the Seasonal 
Naive baseline was affected by differences in the timing and magnitude of 
influenza activity between seasons. The Negative Binomial models showed 
deviations from observed peak intensity in some periods. Although Gradient 
Boosting achieved the lowest MAE, its smoother predictions may not capture 
every rapid increase or peak accurately. Its overall ranking should therefore 
be interpreted alongside RMSE and in-season performance, since different metrics 
emphasise different aspects of forecast error.

The convergence diagnostics for Models 1 and 2 identified no non-converged fits, 
fitting warnings, or fitting errors across the evaluated forecast origins. These 
findings support the numerical reliability of the fitted models within the 
diagnostic procedure, but do not establish that the models are universally 
adequate or accurate.

Overall, **Model 3 (Gradient Boosting) is the preferred model among those evaluated when selection is based on MAE**. 
Nevertheless, the findings are limited to the three test seasons and the 
available surveillance data. Historical data backfilling means that the exact 
information available at each original forecast date could not be verified. 
Future work should examine additional seasons, compare performance consistently 
across MAE and RMSE, and investigate whether improvements in peak detection can 
be achieved without sacrificing overall forecast accuracy..
